title: The Chicago Historical Society concerts and second-class musicians
summary: DeMichael recalls being unable to hire both locals for 1963 concerts; Saunders says Local 208 members were treated as second class.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I remember in about '63, when Petrillo was still in --

-- power, and the Chicago Historical Society wanted to do a series of historical jazz concerts. I was the narrator and arranged for the bands. And we wanted to use black and white musicians. But since -- and it was a trust fund.
And they said, you must use Local 10 musicians. We wanted to use Local 208, also.

No, no. See, and we couldn't understand how we were paying more taxes and we were paying the same joining fees and whatnot, and we didn't have the same privileges. So it made us like second-class musicians, and we couldn't understand how you could have two locals in one jurisdiction in the same jurisdiction.
And these things would go on.
Well, the merging of the two locals in Chicago led then to a lot of other mergers.
Right, they merged all over the country.
That was during the civil rights movement, the heyday of the movement.
